rows.evidence: Q1: Sections III-IV: authors implemented a prototype SWARM system (moisture meters, solenoid valves, software) on a 250 ft x 80 ft groundnut farm in Kuppam, Andhra Pradesh, and tested it for about 1.5 months (end Feb to mid Apr 2006). Q2: Table V and Section V: water applied was 490 mm under SWARM versus 540 mm under the manual system (exact requirement 420 mm); urea 37.8 kg vs 39 kg; authors state manual supplies 129% of water requirement while SWARM delivers 117%, a direct 12% wastage avoided, and about 3% of fertilizer saved. Q8: Section III.B: authors state they could not obtain the SPAD-502 and instead took leaves to a lab twice a day and keyed in chlorophyll values via a USB keypad to simulate the sensor; they could not obtain satellite images and used a sample image; Section IV: values presented were measured only until 11 April during a 1.5-month test on a small-scale implementation.
rows.notes: Own evidence is a single-season, single-farm comparison of total water and urea applied by SWARM versus manual management (Table V); the design of the manual comparison is not described. Soil moisture was sensed to trigger irrigation but no soil water data are reported as results, so Q4 is no. Single method, single site, single crop, no dispersion statistics. Q8 is a cautious yes based on explicitly acknowledged substitutions (lab chlorophyll readings instead of real-time sensor, sample image instead of satellite image) and small-scale, short-duration testing; these are stated restrictions of the implementation rather than a formal limitations discussion.

notes: Conference paper (IEEE 2006) with some OCR garbling in Table IV and the future research section; results in Table V are readable. The study is a prototype demonstration with minimal experimental design description.
